title: Strided KV Compression + Prefetch Fusion (sketch)
body:
Context:
This note explores a hybrid approach to reduce tail latency and memory pressure for long-context serving by combining: (1) lightweight strided prefetch policies that prioritize hot KV slabs, (2) compact per-slab compression (low-bit quantization + small dictionary) to reduce GPU DRAM residency, and (3) fuse-friendly memory layout so FlashAttention kernels can stream keys/values with minimal unpack overhead. The goal is an incremental, low-risk change we can prototype in the serving runtime and validate end-to-end latency improvements for typical chat workloads.

Motivation / problem statement:
- Long conversational histories (8k+ tokens) push KV cache residency and increase page faults / PCIe copies for paged-KV designs.
- Aggressive prefetching reduces page faults but increases memory pressure and can increase average token latency if large slabs are brought in unnecessarily.
- Per-request latency budgets (<50ms for gen) are sensitive to any CPU/GPU unpack or decode work in the hot path.
- Current paged-KV layout interleaves metadata and values in a way that complicates fused attention kernels which expect contiguous QKV memory.

High-level proposal:
1) Strided hot-slab prefetcher: maintain a light-weight hotness estimator per-slab based on request prefixes and token reuse. Instead of bringing contiguous ranges of pages, we pull a strided set of slabs (e.g., every Nth slab in the recent window) that gives better coverage of the frequently-hit KV rows while keeping memory footprint bounded. This reduces the number of stale pages in memory for multi-session workloads.
2) Per-slab compact serialization: on host-side, compress KV slabs with a mixed strategy: a fast 4-bit group-quant + 8-bit residuals when necessary, and a tiny LZ-like micro-dictionary for repeating patterns (common in embedding tails / positional embeddings). Compress streams are stored on SSD/host; when prefetched we perform a top-of-queue lightweight decode to an on-device staging buffer.
3) Fusion-aware slab layout: write prefetched slabs into a GPU buffer with an attention-friendly layout (contiguous K vectors, contiguous V vectors, aligned to 128B lanes). Include an on-GPU header that indicates if slab is exact (no decompression required) or compressed (decompressed in place). Kernels (FlashAttention variant) will check header flags and pick the optimized execution path.

Micro-architecture / kernel notes:
- Add a tiny on-GPU decompressor kernel optimized for 4-bit group quant. It should be low-latency and use vectorized loads + tensor/core where possible. Target decompress time < 1.5us per 4k-token slab on A100 for 16k context.
- For path where slabs are uncompressed, ensure the fused attention kernel reads KV in our contiguous layout to avoid scatter/gather. Minimize extra index math in the inner loop.
- Provide a combined kernel that can accept a mixed buffer: some lanes read pre-decompressed memory, other lanes call the small decompressor inline (cooperative threads). This avoids additional kernel launches for heterogeneous slab mixes.
- Keep kernel fallback: if a slab is missing, fall back to the existing paged-KV fetch (host->device memcpy) and mark it for higher hotness score.

Prefetch policy sketch:
- Hotness estimator: exponentially weighted moving average keyed by (model, session_id, token_prefix_hash). Increment on hit, decay periodically.
- Stride selection: adapt stride based on estimated reuse density. High reuse -> smaller stride (more contiguous pulls). Low reuse -> larger stride. Default starting stride = 4 for chat workloads.
- Budgeting: each model instance has a per-GPU slab budget (configurable). Prefetcher keeps a soft cap and evicts the least hot slabs (considering compression ratio and decode cost).

Operational considerations:
- Instrumentation: track per-slab hit/miss, decode/time, memory residency, and token-latency contribution. Add events for 'prefetch-decode' and 'in-kernel-decompress' to tracing.
- Metrics to collect: tail latency (p95/p99) for generation, percent of tokens served with decompressed-on-GPU vs pre-expanded data, average GPU memory saved (bytes), and additional CPU load for decode.
- Canary plan: rollout to dedicated GPUs with controlled traffic split. Start with read-only experiments (simulate decode without activating fused kernel) to validate timing assumptions.

Experiments / expected numbers (pilot targets):
- Baseline: current paged-KV streaming: median token latency = 9.6ms, p99 = 48ms on A100 with 16k context.
- Hypothesis A (strided prefetch w/o compression): reduce p99 by ~15–25% due to fewer large host->device fetches per request, small median regression +1–2% due to prefetch overhead.
- Hypothesis B (add compact 4-bit with on-device decompress): reduce GPU DRAM footprint by ~30–50%, target p99 reduction additional 10–15% as more useful slabs can be resident; decompress overhead aimed <3% of median token latency.
- Failure modes: decompressor stalls, decode CPU overhead saturates host, or compression artifacts that materially change model outputs (need evaluation on quality).

Quality guardrails:
- Start with lossless or near-lossless configurations (8-bit or 4-bit+8-bit residual). Keep a metric pipeline to compare model logits/eval prompts to detect regressions. If KL divergence on a holdout prompt set exceeds threshold, revert compression profile.

Integration plan & rough milestones:
- Week 1–2: prototype host-side serializer + strided prefetch simulation in runtime (no kernel changes). Collect hotness traces on live traffic. (Owners: Aisha, Marcus)
- Week 3–4: implement GPU slab layout + minimal decompressor kernel; add tracing hooks. Bench microdecode perf. (Owner: Diego)
- Week 5–6: modify FlashAttention fork to accept layout and add mixed-path execution. Run synthetic end-to-end latency tests. (Owners: eng-serving-runtime + ML infra)
- Week 7–8: small canary on dedicated cluster, collect metrics + quality checks, iterate.

Open questions / risks:
- Compression quality vs speed: what quantization schema gives best decode-speed/quality tradeoff for our open models? Need sweep.
- Kernel complexity: is the mixed-path kernel maintainable? If it complicates our FlashAttention fork too much, consider an explicit decompress-then-run approach with batched decompression.
- Memory fragmentation: strided prefetching could cause fragmentation on-device; need eviction heuristics that coalesce slabs.
- Multi-model GPU: per-model slab budgets and protections to prevent noisy neighbors stealing memory.

Next steps (actionable):
- Instrument hotness traces with 48-hour sample, attach to GH issue GH: redwood-inference/serving-runtime#1864.
- Schedule microbench: timing of 4-bit group-decompress on A100 and H100 images. (Diego)
- Run small quality sweep on 50 prompts with 8-bit and 4-bit+resid configs to measure deviation. (Sophia)

Notes to self / rough TODO list:
- Add proto flags: --enable-strided-prefetch, --kv-slab-compression-profile.
- Keep config safe default: disabled in hosted for now, opt-in on Dedicated.
- Cross-reference with storage team on SSD bandwidth assumptions for compressed reads.

This is a sketch — intended to be concrete enough to start a prototype while leaving room for iteration. Comments/alternative ideas welcome: e.g., run-length encoded deltas for positional slabs, or hash-based microcache for very hot rows.
